posts.cooked: 假设，我有50个账户，其中一些账户买了一些金额的ckb，锁定后具备投票资格，那么是否可以发起一个提案，用其中一些账户点赞，再投票，然后盗取DAO资金？，如果50个账户是我的50个朋友呢？或者其他可能性。，那么是不是DAO可以被以这样的方式随意推动提案成功并盗取资金？

Yeah, it’s possible, but they also have to have enough CKB to win the vote.

There’s enough community members here, some of which have very high amounts of CKB who would probably step in an make it hard for any obvious scams or manipulation.

There’s also been a few times already where there’s been obvious manipulation of the proposal liking system by sockpuppets and ‘friends’ which have been stopped.

But it’s definitely an situation that we need to be aware of.

posts.name: zz_tovarishch
posts.cooked:
Hi Fai

Fai:

只看到投出的钱，而DAO项目后续有人在跟踪吗？

按照目前Community Fund DAO的规则，资助类提案如果有申请initial fund，那么在投票通过后，会由委员会进行打款。而后续里程碑支付则是按照项目提交Milestone 报告，依照以下规则，由社区进行审阅、提出问题。

CKB Community Fund DAO Rules and Process
  • 社区成员也有权监督申请团队的工作成效和资金使用情况，并在论坛中发表评论或进行讨论。

若里程碑报告提交后一段时间，社区没有更多意见后，委员会会进行里程碑款项的支付。因为现行规则中对于社区审阅的时长没有明确声明，所以在实践中社区审阅期按照2周进行，即里程碑报告提交后，若社区没有更多意见的时间达到2周，委员会会进行打款。

不可否认的是，现行规则有非常多改善的空间，期待大家的更多讨论、治理实践，乃至发起元规则提案。

posts.cooked:
Fai:

Despite facing clear opposition from a large number of community members, it still managed to push through by relying on insider networks and the backing of some veteran members.

this is the nature of a community. People who have invested significant amounts of time in something have a high degree of influence, a high degree of information and feel strongly about what they are trying to accomplish.

There is no changing this reality, only being responsible about how the influence is exercised, lessons were learned from the experience. While I do expect that some things about the Rosen Bridge proposal will never happen again, the basic premise we are operating under remains the same.

Ultimately the proposal passed a coin vote, this is the mechanism that decides whether a proposal passes or fails.

It was already addressed in another post (forgive me for not taking the time to dig it up) that an employee of the Nervos Foundation provided an endorsement beyond the scope they should have as an employee.

The argument over 1) if a coin vote is a good idea or not, or 2) about improper influence from those in positions of authority are reasonable, however these 2 concerns should not be combined to question the legitimacy of a proposal passing.

The vote was legitimate, this is what is important. If you disagree with the outcome of a coin vote, lets discuss that on a separate thread for improving DAO processes.

Fai:

And the result? Some people left in disappointment, the project ultimately fell apart, and the DAO wasted precious treasury funds — a lesson that left everyone worse off.

Hey @Fai, the integration is on hold, not abandoned: I covered the details in the Rosen thread.

The DAO paid only the first milestone: $15k for the technical assessment and development plan, public in the tracker. The other $50k comes only with the testbed and mainnet releases: no release, no payment. The work since then caught a bridge risk before any CKB user funds were exposed.

About that risk: each Guard (the operators who jointly sign bridge payouts) trusts one data source for deposits, by default a public RPC. If enough Guards read the same source and it lies, a fake deposit can get paid out. I raised it with Rosen: they prefer improving their anomaly detection, so I asked whether it can block the payout in that case. I’m waiting for their answer. Releasing on mainnet before this is solved would put user funds at risk.

Love & Peace, Phroi

Questioning how the Community Fund operates is part of participating in governance. You can disagree with the tone of posts on X, but that leaves the questions I raised about the DAO unanswered. People should be able to raise those questions here without first having to prove that their involvement is meaningful.

I agree that builders need room to experiment and that some experiments will fail. My concern is what happens after the initial work is done. Is the project still being used? Is anyone maintaining it? What did the team learn that could inform future funding decisions? A brief public update would help the community answer those questions and learn from experiments that fell short.

The same goes for voting. Prominent community members are free to endorse proposals, and other members are equally free to question the weight those endorsements carry. When an endorsement can sway a vote, explaining the reasons behind it gives everyone else something concrete to evaluate and challenge.

The DAO’s four years of experience give us a basis for improving how it works. If this forum is focused on action, a good place to start is making project outcomes easier to review and funding decisions easier to scrutinize.
